title: Musa's du'a at the well
hook: my Lord, I am in need of whatever good You send me (28:24)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ibrahim's du'a, and your line, accept my prayer. Today, a prayer from a man with nothing left in his hands.

Musa is running. In Egypt, he stepped into a fight to defend a man of his people, struck the other man once, and the man died. Now Pharaoh's people are looking for him. He leaves alone, heading toward Madyan, with only a hope: maybe my Lord will guide me on the right road, he says. He arrives at a well, exhausted. And before he does anything for himself, he notices two young women standing back from the crowd.

Surah al-Qasas, verses twenty-three and twenty-four. A crowd of shepherds is watering their flocks. Two women hold their animals back. Musa asks what's wrong. They say: we can't water until the shepherds have gone, and our father is a very old man. So he waters their flock for them. Then he turns aside into the shade, and there, in Pickthall's translation, he prays: "My Lord! I am needy of whatever good Thou sendest down for me." Look how little he specifies. Not food, though he's hungry. Not safety, though he's hunted. Not a home or a wife. Just: whatever good You send, I need it. The Arabic word is faqir, poor, in need. And khayr, good, is left wide open. He doesn't tell Allah what the answer should look like. And the order: first he helps, then he sits in the shade and asks. The answer comes in the very next verse. One of the two women comes back, walking shyly, and says: my father invites you, to reward you for watering for us. Food, shelter, work, and later a marriage. The Qur'an doesn't name the old father; some commentators said he was the prophet Shu'ayb, and others disagreed. What the verses do show is how much good can arrive through one open request, prayed in the shade, by a tired man who had just helped two strangers.
screen: `HE WATERS, THEN SITS IN THE SHADE.`

segments.voice: Sit as if you've just come in out of the sun, into shade, and bring to mind what you need right now, noticing whether you've already decided what the answer should be. Loosen it, and hold the need open. If you pray, say Musa's words, rabbi inni lima anzalta ilayya min khayrin faqir, my Lord, I am in need of whatever good You send me; if not, just sit with open hands.
Faqir. Poor, in need: Musa's prayer at the well, my Lord, I'm in need of whatever good You send, with nothing specified. Today's word.
Your line: in need of any good. First he helped, then he asked. That's six hundred ninety.

howItsDone: Some Muslims say Musa's du'a (28:24) in times of need, job searches, or uncertainty, leaving the shape of the answer to Allah.

original.note: Arabic, 28:24: my Lord, I am in need of whatever good You send down to me.

trapdoor: what you thought: Musa's story is the sea and the staff.
what it means: before all that, a hunted man helped two strangers, sat in the shade, and asked for any good at all.
what a scholar hears: faqir and an open-ended khayr; the answer arrives in 28:25; the father's identity (Shu'ayb, some say) is debated by commentators.

chat.says: What did Musa pray for at the well, when he had nothing?
options: Whatever good You send, I need it. He left the answer wide open.
Food, and a safe place to hide from Pharaoh's people, named exactly.
A wife and a home of his own; he asked for both by name.
chat.meaning: 28:24: My Lord! I am needy of whatever good Thou sendest down for me. Khayr, good, is left open.

Madyan.meaning: the land Musa fled to from Egypt

Shu'ayb.meaning: a prophet some commentators name as the old father
